content_metadata.description: A tutorial video featuring a man demonstrating how to collimate a Newtonian telescope using a laser collimator.

qAndA.answer: The man is collimating a Newtonian telescope.
qAndA.question: What type of telescope is being used in the video?

qAndA.answer: The man tests the laser collimator to ensure that the laser is pointing straight and true. If it is not accurate, it will not collimate the telescope properly.
qAndA.question: Why does the man test the laser collimator before using it?

qAndA.answer: He used thumb screws at the back of the scope.
qAndA.question: What does the man use to adjust the primary mirror?
What does the man do to make it easier to see the laser on the target at the back of the telescope?

qAndA.answer: He tightens up the locking screws.
qAndA.question: What does the man do to make sure that the primary mirror does not move once it is collimated?

timecoded_text_to_speech.text: Hi everyone and welcome back to the channel. I'm going to talk today about how I
Colomate my Newtonian scope, in this case of 130 pds. I use a laser
columnator. These do get a bit of bad press but as long as they're accurate
you shouldn't have too many problems and we can check that before we use it.
Some columnators come with adjustment screws around the outside and I would
suggest that if you're going to get one get one with these so that if there is
any problems with its accuracy you can adjust it. So the first thing to do is
check that the columnator is true so what we're going to do is fix this into a
position pointing out a wall. I use a vice for this and what we're looking to
do is just get it a good distance from a wall with a point that we can look
at. Turn the columnator on and then very slowly rotate the columnator,
watching the laser point on the wall. We want it to rotate but stay in roughly
the same position. If it makes a larger circle then we know that the laser is not
pointing straight and true and won't columnate your scope very accurately so
you will need to make adjustments. If however we're happy with the laser we can
now move on to columnating the scope. Place the laser into the focus tube and then
what we need to do is observe down the front of the scope at the circle that's
on the primary mirror and observe where the laser is hitting that target. Here you
can see the laser is hitting the top left hand corner of the circle so we need
to make adjustments to get that laser into the center. We make those adjustments
by these screws at the front of the scope. You may have Allen key bolts here
that require an Allen key to turn them. I've replaced these with a product
known as Bob's knobs and I'll put a link in the description of where you can
get them from but these then become thumb screws and make
columnation a lot easier. So proceed by making very very small turns of these
screws, undoing one first and then slightly tightening up the slack with the
other two and just move the laser around and you want to get the point in the
dead center of that small circle on the primary mirror. Make sure you don't
make any large turns they're not needed and when you are finished and you are
happy that the laser is in the center check to make sure that none of the screws
are loose and that they're all nipped up. That's the secondary mirror
columnated and now we need to move to the primary mirror so we need to move to
the rear of the scope and we need to at the same time as being able to access
these screws at the back of the scope be able to also see the target on the
columnator. We have six screws at the back three are locking screws the longer
ones so we can just loosen these off and we're going to make small adjustments to
the largest thumb screws to move the laser to the correct part on the target.
So I'm just going to dim the light so that we can see the laser a bit easier and
then making small adjustments of these screws at the back moving the primary
mirror we're going to make the laser disappear into the hole on the target. Again
small movements take your time with it and once you're happy that the laser is
in the center gently do up the locking screws. Now these can move the laser
so be aware of that don't over tighten them and just lock everything up so that
the primary mirror won't move. Once this is in place and we're happy that the
laser is in the center of that target we need to check the front of the scope
again and make sure that the first check we did is still in place that the
laser is in the dot of the circle and if it is then everything's good and the
scope is collimated if it isn't just repeat the steps until you have the laser
inside the two targets. I hope this has helped and if you do have any questions
please let me know in the comment section. If you like the content please consider
liking and subscribing and until next time I'd like to wish you all clear skies.
